Key observations from the test image:
- Split/opened soybean stems showing bleached white interior
- Large black masses (sclerotia) embedded inside the stem cavities
- Dead, dried stem tissue with bleached white appearance
- Multiple stems shown cross-sectioned

This strongly points to **White Mold** — the hallmark feature is black sclerotia inside bleached white stems. Let me verify with reference images.
The charcoal rot shows gray stems with fine specks (microsclerotia), quite different from the large black masses in the test image. Let me check a few more candidates to reach the required 21 views.
The Fusarium reference (top-right) looks very similar to the test image — bleached white split stems with large black masses inside. Let me view more references to reach 21 and resolve this.

I've now viewed 26 reference images. None of the other candidates (leaf spot diseases, viral diseases, root rots) match the test image at all.

**Analysis:**
- **Test image**: Multiple soybean stems split longitudinally, showing bleached white exterior and **large, irregular black masses** packed inside the stem cavities — against a background of a living soybean field
- These large (cm-scale), irregular, hard black bodies inside hollow bleached stems are **sclerotia** — the resting structures of *Sclerotinia sclerotiorum*
- This is the definitive diagnostic feature of **White Mold**
- The Fusarium reference collage did show a quadrant with similar-looking split stems, but Fusarium causes brown vascular discoloration, not large discrete sclerotia inside hollow stems
- White Mold description explicitly states: *"characteristic black sclerotia embedded within white fluffy mold on stems and inside stems"* and *"Dry dead stems develop a bleached white appearance"*

The visual evidence is unambiguous: bleached white stem + large black sclerotia inside = White Mold.

No other soybean disease produces large discrete black sclerotia inside hollow stems.
